newsitem.title: LEBANON: Radical Moslem cleric launches protest in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Radical Moslem cleric launches protest in Lebanon.

text.p: A radical Shi'ite cleric on Friday launched a civil disobedience campaign against the Lebanese government at a rally of several thousand supporters in the eastern Bekaa Valley.
"We declare civil disobedience," Sheikh Sobhi Tufaili, a former leader of the pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God), said in a fiery speech in the ancient town of Baalbek.

About 3,000 people packing the town's main square raised their fists and shouted in support of Tufaili, who has called on Bekaa Valley residents to join his "hunger revolt" to put pressure on the government to ease poverty in the region.
The Bekaa has suffered economically from a crackdown on illegal drug crops which generated some $150 million in annual income during the 1975-90 civil war.

Tufaili told the crowd to stop paying taxes and other bills and reiterated a threat to spread his campaign across Lebanon if the government failed to meet his demands. He has said he would lead a march on Beirut and besiege the residences of Lebanon's top political leaders.

His campaign has alarmed the authorities in Beirut and triggered debates in Lebanese newspapers. President Elias Hrawi has threatened Tufaili with legal action and accused him of threatening to return Lebanon to chaos.

Authorities tightened security on roads leading to Baalbek on Friday. Lebanese army forces sat on armoured personnel carriers at key intersections outside the town but made no attempt to stop people reaching the rally.
The authorities allowed Tufaili and his supporters freedom to hold their rally in Baalbek's central square with only a limited presence of police armed with automatic rifles.

Tufaili, 51, was flanked by plainclothes bodyguards with pistols tucked into their trousers. They stood on a platform in front of the Baalbek serail (government house) which was draped in a huge black cloth with a white inscription saying: "This is the grave of the Lebanese government. God damn its soul."

Tufaili called on the crowd, which overflowed from the square onto roofs, to press ahead with civil disobedience. "Patience has its limits. They closed the door on you. They have turned this country into a desert," he said.

Dressed in the black cloak and white turban of a Shi'ite cleric, he added: "Oh people who live in this mafia state, we want our full rights. We will impose our rights. This is the day of the hunger revolt.
"We must move ahead to other stations. You will find fear but be brave men."
The crowd, some of whom held pieces of bread up on wooden sticks to symbolise shortage of food and hunger, shouted "God is great," and cursed the Lebanese government.

"Death to Hariri," they said, referring to billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri. "Down with the government," they yelled as teenagers with black bandanas around their foreheads kept the crowd away from Tufaili.
Members of the crowd said they would participate in the civil disobedience campaign.
"This revolt is correct. I will not pay my bills until this government falls. They are liars," said Mahmoud al-Amin, an unemployed young man in the crowd.
Abdullah Ismail, one of Tufaili's bodyguards, was more forceful. "I am willing to shoot this government," he said, grabbing his pistol.

The Beirut government allocated 150 billion Lebanese pounds ($97 million) to develop the Bekaa Valley after Tufaili announced his campaign. Beirut newspapers implied the move was designed to undermine the campaign.
